lead: This unit takes a plain silicon wafer to a finished CMOS chip and then shows how a designer draws that chip: every layer, every mask and every spacing rule. After it you can name the process behind any layer you see in a cross-section, choose between n-well, p-well and twin-tub, read a stick diagram, and explain latch-up and the layout habits that prevent it.
about: This unit is about how a CMOS chip is built and how a designer describes that build in geometry. Chapter 2.1 covers the three thermal processes: oxidation, diffusion and ion implantation. Chapter 2.2 shows how patterns are printed, etched and filled. Chapter 2.3 puts those steps in order as the nMOS and CMOS process flow. Chapter 2.4 compares the p-well, n-well and twin-tub ways of placing both transistors on one wafer. Chapter 2.5 adds a bipolar transistor to CMOS. Chapters 2.6 and 2.7 turn the process into drawing rules and stick diagrams. Chapter 2.8 closes with latch-up, the failure that layout must prevent.

chapters.idea: Three unit processes change the silicon itself: oxidation grows an oxide, diffusion and ion implantation put dopant atoms into it.
chapters.depth: Thermal oxidation: wet versus dry, the Deal-Grove model and its linear and parabolic limits, why gate oxide is grown dry and slow while field oxide is grown wet and thick. Diffusion: Fick's first and second law, predeposition versus drive-in, the diffusion length 2√(Dt), strong temperature dependence. Ion implantation: dose in cm⁻², energy in keV, projected range Rp, the Gaussian profile, channeling and tilt, masking by oxide or resist, and the anneal that repairs lattice damage. Typical numbers: oxidation and diffusion 900-1100 °C, implant 30-200 keV. Some syllabi group these as 'thermal processes'.

figure.title: One masked doping step
figure.aria: Block diagram of one doping step: wafer, thermal oxidation, a patterned resist window, a diffusion drive-in, an ion implant and a final anneal.

chapters.example: At 1000 °C the diffusion coefficient of phosphorus in silicon is D = 3×10⁻¹⁴ cm²/s. A drive-in lasts t = 1 hour = 3600 s. (a) Find the diffusion length L = 2√(Dt). (b) Is the junction shallower or deeper than 0.5 μm? (c) How long would 0.5 μm take? Answer: (a) L = 2√(3×10⁻¹⁴ × 3600) = 2√(1.08×10⁻¹⁰) cm = 2 × 1.04×10⁻⁵ cm = 0.21 μm. (b) Shallower. (c) t = (0.25×10⁻⁴)²/D = 6.25×10⁻¹⁰ / 3×10⁻¹⁴ = 2.08×10⁴ s ≈ 5.8 hours.
chapters.trap: Mixing dose (cm⁻², atoms per unit area) with concentration (cm⁻³). Also: diffusion is isotropic, so it spreads sideways under the mask exactly as far as it goes down; implantation is not, and that is why it makes shallow junctions.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: donors, acceptors, carrier concentration and the MOS structure.
chapters.leave: The lithography that opens the mask window goes to 2.2, the full step order to 2.3, and junction capacitance to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: A pattern is printed in resist, then the layer below is either cut away (etch) or built up (deposition).
chapters.depth: Photolithography as a loop: clean, coat resist, soft bake, align the mask, expose, develop, then etch or deposit, then strip. Positive versus negative resist, contact/proximity/projection printing, mask versus reticle, resolution R = k·λ/NA and depth of focus, and why a shorter wavelength and a higher NA fight each other. Etching: wet (isotropic, undercut) versus dry (RIE, anisotropic), selectivity, endpoint detection, over-etch. Deposition: LPCVD, PECVD, sputtering, evaporation, epitaxy (a single-crystal silicon layer grown on the wafer, used as the lightly doped collector layer in 2.5), and CMP to flatten before the next layer. Some syllabi call this group 'pattern transfer'. Electron-beam inspection (beam-specimen interactions) is in a few syllabi.

figure.title: The lithography loop
figure.aria: Block diagram of the photolithography loop: clean, coat resist, soft bake, align and expose, develop, etch or deposit, strip resist.

chapters.example: A projection printer has wavelength 248 nm, NA = 0.5 and process factor k = 0.6. (a) Find the smallest printable feature R = k·λ/NA. (b) Find the depth of focus DOF = λ/(2NA²). (c) Repeat both for NA = 0.6. Answer: (a) R = 0.6 × 248 / 0.5 = 298 nm ≈ 0.30 μm. (b) DOF = 248 / (2 × 0.25) = 496 nm ≈ 0.50 μm. (c) R = 0.6 × 248 / 0.6 = 248 nm, DOF = 248 / (2 × 0.36) = 344 nm: better resolution, worse depth of focus.
chapters.trap: Wet etching undercuts the mask, so the etched hole is wider than the window. Drawing a square etch profile is wrong. Also keep positive resist (exposed part dissolves) and negative resist (exposed part stays) apart.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1: the oxide grown there is the layer the resist patterns.
chapters.leave: The full mask order goes to 2.3, automated rule checking to Unit 5, and wire capacitance and delay to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A process flow is just the mask sequence: each mask adds one layer or one doping, in an order fixed by temperature and alignment.
chapters.depth: Start from the wafer and follow the masks. Isolation (LOCOS versus shallow trench), gate oxidation, poly deposition and doping, the self-aligned source/drain implant that uses the poly gate as its own mask, spacers and lightly doped drains, contact and via, metallisation, passivation and pad opening. Do the short nMOS-only flow first, then the CMOS flow, which adds wells and two separate source/drain masks so n+ and p+ never see the same implant. Name the front-end (transistors) and back-end (wiring) of the line. Cover MOS memory processes in one paragraph only, as a pointer.

figure.title: CMOS mask sequence
figure.aria: Block diagram of a CMOS flow, one mask after another from the well mask to the metal mask.

chapters.example: A CMOS process uses these masks, one lithography step each: n-well, active, poly, n+ source/drain, p+ source/drain, contact, metal 1, via, metal 2, pad. (a) How many lithography steps? (b) A die is 0.5 cm² and the line has D = 1 defect/cm²; use Y = e^(−A·D) for yield. (c) How many steps if metal 2 is dropped? Answer: (a) 10. (b) Y = e^(−0.5 × 1) = 0.607, about 61%. (c) 8, since the via and metal 2 masks both go.
chapters.trap: Saying source and drain are 'diffused through a window'. They are implanted with the poly gate acting as the mask, and that self-alignment is what keeps gate and source/drain from drifting apart.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.1 and 2.2; Unit 1 for what a transistor needs.
chapters.leave: Well variants go to 2.4, bipolar steps to 2.5, memory cells to Unit 4 and FinFETs to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Both transistors need opposite body doping, so one of them must sit inside a well; the three well processes differ in which one, and how independently each can be doped.
chapters.depth: p-well: NMOS in a p-well inside an n-substrate, PMOS in the substrate. n-well: PMOS in an n-well inside a p-substrate, NMOS in the substrate; the variant most processes use, because the substrate can be tied to VSS at low resistance, which helps latch-up, and the NMOS keeps the better substrate. Twin-tub: separate n-well and p-well doped independently, so both threshold voltages and both body-effect coefficients can be set, at the cost of one extra mask. Compare mask count, well doping, substrate resistance, latch-up immunity and which device is buried. Give triple-well and silicon-on-insulator one short paragraph; only a few universities teach SOI.

figure.aria: Tree diagram: a p-substrate holding an n-well with the PMOS, an NMOS placed directly in the substrate, and a p+ substrate tap.

chapters.example: In an n-well process μn = 500 cm²/V·s and μp = 200 cm²/V·s. (a) For a symmetric inverter, find Wp/Wn. (b) With L = 0.5 μm and Wn = 2 μm, find Wp. (c) Which transistor sits inside the well, and which carrier sets the speed? Answer: (a) Wp/Wn = μn/μp = 500/200 = 2.5. (b) Wp = 5 μm. (c) The PMOS sits in the n-well; electrons in the NMOS set the speed, which is why the PMOS must be 2.5 times wider.
chapters.trap: Thinking the n-well process puts the NMOS in a well. It does not: the NMOS sits in the p-substrate and only the PMOS is inside the well.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.3; Unit 1 for threshold voltage and the body effect.
chapters.leave: The bipolar structure goes to 2.5, latch-up itself to 2.8, memory processes to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: BiCMOS builds the CMOS flow first and then adds a vertical NPN on the same die, so one chip has both high input impedance and high drive.
chapters.depth: Bipolar basics first: the vertical NPN, emitter-base-collector, current gain β, why a buried n+ layer and a thin n-epitaxial layer are needed to cut collector resistance, and junction isolation. Then BiCMOS: build the CMOS exactly as in 2.4 and add the NPN with three or four extra masks: buried layer, base, emitter, and often a deep collector sinker. What it buys: high transconductance and drive from the bipolar, low power and high density from CMOS. What it costs: more masks, longer cycle time, lower yield, a tighter thermal budget. Uses: RF front ends, high-speed drivers, mixed-signal and power chips. Bipolar IC technology alone gets a short comparison.

figure.title: BiCMOS flow
figure.aria: Block diagram of the BiCMOS flow: buried layer, epitaxy, CMOS wells and gates, then the NPN base, emitter, contacts and metal.

chapters.example: An NPN in BiCMOS is biased at collector current 2 mA with β = 100; thermal voltage is 26 mV. (a) Find the base current and gm = Ic/VT. (b) A MOSFET at the same 2 mA has overdrive VGS − VT = 0.5 V, so gm = 2Ic/(VGS − VT). Compare the two. Answer: (a) Ib = 2 mA/100 = 20 μA; gm = 2 mA / 26 mV = 77 mA/V. (b) gm = 2 × 2 mA / 0.5 V = 8 mA/V. The bipolar has about 9.6 times the transconductance at the same current.
chapters.trap: Treating BiCMOS as 'CMOS plus one transistor'. The buried layer, the epitaxy and the sinker are what make a fast vertical NPN, and they cost masks, yield and thermal budget.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.4 for the wells; Unit 1 for MOSFET behaviour.
chapters.leave: Small-signal bipolar models belong to an analog course, and ECL logic is outside this unit.

chapters.idea: Design rules are the minimum widths, spacings and overlaps that keep a drawn shape manufacturable, written as multiples of a single unit λ.
chapters.depth: Rules exist because of mask misalignment, etch bias and the finite resolution of the printer. Explain λ (the scalable unit set by the foundry, often half the smallest drawn feature) and micron rules. Give the rule families: minimum width, minimum spacing, minimum overlap, enclosure, extension, and separation between unrelated layers. Then a small worked rule set for active, poly, contact and metal 1, and how to convert λ to μm. Say that a design rule checker tests every rule by computer and that real rule sets run to hundreds of rules. Some syllabi call these 'scalable design rules'. A short note on estimating wire resistance from sheet resistance.

figure.title: Rule set used in the example
figure.aria: Table of layout rules with minimum width in the first column and minimum spacing in the second, for metal, poly, diffusion and contact.

chapters.example: Take λ = 0.5 μm with rules: metal width 3λ, metal spacing 3λ, poly width 2λ, contact 2λ × 2λ, metal enclosure of a contact 1λ. (a) Give the minimum metal width and the minimum metal pitch in μm. (b) Give the minimum poly width. (c) A transistor has W = 8λ and L = 2λ; find its gate area and its gate capacitance with C_ox = 2.3 fF/μm². Answer: (a) 3λ = 1.5 μm; pitch = 3λ + 3λ = 6λ = 3.0 μm. (b) 2λ = 1.0 μm. (c) W = 4 μm, L = 1 μm, area = 4 μm², C = 4 × 2.3 = 9.2 fF.
chapters.trap: Using λ for both the layout unit and the lithography wavelength. In a layout answer λ is the unit; write the printer wavelength in nm in 2.2.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.3 for which layers exist and 2.2 for why alignment errors happen.
chapters.leave: Parasitic capacitance and resistance and their effect on delay go to Unit 3; rule-checking tools and physical design to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A stick diagram is a topology sketch of a gate: one line per layer, no dimensions, where every crossing of poly and diffusion is a transistor.
chapters.depth: Conventions: one line style or colour per layer (diffusion, poly, metal, contact), VDD and VSS rails as metal at the top and bottom, no absolute dimensions, only order and crossings. The rule that matters: a poly line crossing a diffusion line is a transistor, so an unwanted crossing is an unwanted device. Then the method: write the transistor network (series = AND, parallel = OR), find an Euler path over the edges, draw one diffusion strip per side, and place the poly columns in that same order. Finish with translating the stick diagram to a mask layout with real widths from 2.6.

figure.title: Schematic to stick diagram
figure.aria: Flow from schematic, through the transistor networks and the Euler path, to one diffusion strip per side, the poly columns and the finished stick diagram.

chapters.example: For the CMOS gate y = ¬(a·b + c): (a) write the nMOS and pMOS networks, (b) find an Euler path on each side, (c) state how many diffusion strips and poly columns the stick diagram needs. Answer: (a) nMOS pull-down: a and b in series, with c in parallel across the pair. pMOS pull-up: a and b in parallel, that pair in series with c. (b) Both sides allow the Euler order c, a, b: n-side GND–c–y–a–n1–b–GND, p-side y–c–n2–a–VDD–b–n2. (c) One n-diffusion strip, one p-diffusion strip, three poly columns.
chapters.trap: Letting a poly line cross a diffusion line where no transistor is wanted. In a stick diagram there is no 'just a wire' crossing: the crossing is a device.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.6 for real widths; Unit 3 for reading a CMOS gate as series and parallel networks.
chapters.leave: Full layout, floorplanning, placement and routing go to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: The well, the substrate and the source diffusions form a parasitic p-n-p-n path, and layout must keep its loop gain below one.
chapters.depth: The parasitic path in an n-well process: the p+ source, the n-well and the p-substrate form a pnp; the n+ source, the p-substrate and the n-well form an npn. With R_well and R_sub they make a four-layer p-n-p-n SCR. Triggering: a current spike, input undershoot, radiation, or a supply ramp injecting majority carriers into the substrate. The condition: loop gain β_npn × β_pnp > 1 with the resistors large enough to hold both emitters on. Prevention: substrate and well taps placed close and often, guard rings around the NMOS and PMOS, a low-resistance p+ substrate with a thin epitaxial layer, retrograde wells, shallow trench isolation, and silicide to shunt the parasitic resistances. Mention the standard current-injection latch-up test.

figure.aria: Directed graph of the parasitic npn and pnp transistors closing a loop through the n-well and the p-substrate, each drawn as a collector feeding the other base.

chapters.example: An n-well CMOS inverter has R_sub = 200 Ω and R_well = 1 kΩ, with β_npn = 50 and β_pnp = 20. (a) A spike injects 2 mA into the substrate. Find the substrate drop; the npn emitter needs 0.7 V to turn on. Does it turn on? (b) Repeat for R_sub = 500 Ω. (c) Is the loop regenerative once an emitter is on? Answer: (a) V = 2 mA × 200 Ω = 0.4 V < 0.7 V, so no. (b) V = 2 mA × 500 Ω = 1.0 V > 0.7 V, so the npn turns on. (c) β_npn × β_pnp = 50 × 20 = 1000 > 1, so the loop is regenerative and the chip latches up.
chapters.trap: Believing that adding taps anywhere is enough. What matters is the resistance between the injection point and the tap, so tap spacing and guard rings are the real fix.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.4 and 2.6: well structure and the spacing rules that keep taps close.
chapters.leave: ESD protection circuits are a separate topic; the memory array's own parasitic paths go to Unit 4.
